courses.profile: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
courses.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Genuine business/leadership/finance/legal/economics content; withdrawn from the former business-heavy alternative to restore defining biomedical substance.

courses.profile: This course describes the most widely accepted accounting theory and practice with an emphasis on using and analyzing the information in financial statements. Students learn how to comprehend a typical corporate annual report and to use accounting as a tool in understanding how economic events affect business.
courses.description2: This course describes the most widely accepted accounting theory and practice with an emphasis on using and analyzing the information in financial statements. Students learn how to comprehend a typical corporate annual report and to use accounting as a tool in understanding how economic events affect business.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Financial statements and accounting; enterprise companion rather than biomedical discipline.

courses.profile: This course introduces students to the legal frameworks governing business transactions in a globalized economy. It examines how law shapes cross-border trade, contracts, sales of goods and services, intellectual property, foreign investment, and digital commerce. Emphasis is placed on the practical application of legal rules to real-world business scenarios, as well as on comparative and international perspectives. Through interactive class discussions, problem - based assignments, quizzes, and an arbitration simulation, students develop the analytical and practical skills needed to identify legal risks and design effective solutions in transnational business contexts.
courses.description2: Businesses and entrepreneurs are confronted with legal complexity not only at the domestic level but particularly across divergent legal systems. This course presents a survey of the most essential fields of business law: contracts law, company law, trade law, intellectual property, and dispute resolution. An ultimate aim of the course is to critically examine the impact of globalization and digitization on the development of business law.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Genuine business/leadership/finance/legal/economics content; withdrawn from the former business-heavy alternative to restore defining biomedical substance.

courses.profile: This course develops practical financial decision-making skills through case studies and real-world applications. Students learn to analyze financial data, assess risks, and make informed investment, budgeting, and business decisions that enhance value, financial security, and long-term planning.
courses.description2: This course develops practical financial decision-making skills through case studies and real-world applications. Students learn to analyze financial data, assess risks, and make informed investment, budgeting, and business decisions that enhance value, financial security, and long-term planning.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Genuine business/leadership/finance/legal/economics content; withdrawn from the former business-heavy alternative to restore defining biomedical substance.

courses.profile: This course provides an introduction to the principles of economics. The first part of the course delves into microeconomics concepts, including supply and demand, game theory, theory of consumer behaviour, theory of the firm and market structure. The seco nd part of the course covers macroeconomics, beginning with an exploration of macroeconomics events and fundamental concepts such as aggregate output, unemployment and inflation rate. It then examines the dynamics of goods and financial markets in the short run.
courses.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Genuine business/leadership/finance/legal/economics content; withdrawn from the former business-heavy alternative to restore defining biomedical substance.

courses.profile: This course examines the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy affects efficiency and equity. It explores the rationale for government intervention and key concepts such as market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, p ublic spending, redistribution, and political economy. By combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, the course provides a framework for analysing the economic impact of public policies.
courses.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Genuine business/leadership/finance/legal/economics content; withdrawn from the former business-heavy alternative to restore defining biomedical substance.

courses.profile: In this course you will learn how to function in a 'real-world' design and development environment. Hence, you will work in a group that mimics a design and development (d&d) team as e.g. in industry. The members of a team in this course fulfill roles similarly as occur in industrial d&d teams (e.g. chair person, secretary, ...). A team is responsible for much of its own planning. The functioning of a team involves e.g. preparing agendas for team meetings, taking minutes, planning practical work, maintaining a documentation system, etc. During the course, the instructor will NOT act as chairperson / team leader, but rather as an ‘external consultant'. During the course we will go through the various phases of the development of a consumer product: assessment of customer needs and translating these into a product concept, develop a method to make a product, both on laboratory- as on industrial scale, analyzing environmental impact, analyzing costs and proceeds. In a d&d project and hence in the course, activities are quite varied, and include interviewing potential customers, laboratory experiments, constructing quantitative mathematical model(s) of the working mechanism(s) of a product, constructing a prototype, work out how a product can be produced on an industrial scale, consider protection of intellectual property etc.. In this course, in addition to the more traditional aspects of the d&d process, special attention will be given to sustainability. This involves e.g. the nature of the materials used (natural, recycled, …), lifespan, repairability, 'circularity' etc.
courses.description2: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Consumer product design/development, prototypes, sustainability and basic IP context; no specifically biomedical regulated-product or clinical development project established.

courses.profile: Grounded in academic theory, real-world applications, and case studies, this course unpacks what drives consumers’ behaviour and engagement with brands, and how marketers can build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key concepts related to marketing strategy and consumer psychology and examines external forces influencing reinvention of the Marketing function, including digital and AI-driven marketing. Drawing on the work of Kotler, Aaker, Kapferer and other leading scholars, students will explore real-life case studies, develop marketing plans and learn how to create effective brand strategies for greater consumer engagement.
courses.description2: This course unpacks what drives consumer engagement with brands and how marketers build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key marketing concepts, consumer psychology, AI/technology-driven marketing innovation, and brand and communication strategies. Students will explore real-life case studies, develop a strategic marketing plan and learn how marketers build sustainable brand strategies.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Marketing theory, consumer behaviour, brands and responsible engagement; no biomedical-specific marketing training established.

courses.profile: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.
courses.description2: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Business strategy and digital transformation, rather than laboratory translation.

courses.profile: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas—perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.
courses.description2: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas—perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Customer/market research; not biomedical experimental or clinical research.

courses.profile: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
courses.description2: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
courses.contributionAndLimit: International business institutions, governance and corporate responsibility; organisational context.

courses.profile: In this course, you will develop a new venture idea from the ground up. No prior business experience is required – working in teams you will learn by doing, developing a startup concept from ideation through to the final pitch. Along the way, you will gain essential business and entrepreneurial skills, including design thinking, market validation and business planning. This course fosters creativity, business acumen and collaboration to drive business and social entrepreneurship.
courses.description2: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Venture ideation, design thinking, validation and planning; general enterprise foundation.

courses.profile: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
courses.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
courses.contributionAndLimit: General research design, sampling, statistics and group research; not full longitudinal biomedical competence assessment.

courses.profile: Personal Leadership is an interactive course for Liberal Arts and Sciences students that introduces leadership fundamentals with a focus on self-awareness and practical skills. Through a blend of theory, interaction, and assessments, students will cultivate the tools needed to lead effectively in both personal and professional contexts. The course begins by exploring leadership fundamentals, emphasizing transformational leadership (Bass, 1990) and authentic leadership (Gardner et al., 2021), supported by foundational concepts from Northouse’s Leadership: Theory and Practice (2025), which offers a balanced overview of various leadership models and their applications. Covey’s (2020) The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People: 30th Anniversary Edition provides a foundation for principles such as proactive behavior, prioritization, and fostering collaboration. Students critically analyze these concepts through evolutionary perspectives on adaptive strategies (Lonati & Van Vugt, 2023) and apply Locke and Latham’s (2019) goal-setting theory to develop actionable leadership plans. Self-awareness and emotional intelligence (Goleman, 2021) are central themes, with students engaging in reflective exercises, group discussions, and personality assessments to better understand their strengths, values, and leadership styles. The course maximizes interaction through workshops, group projects, role-playing, and peer feedback sessions, ensuring active engagement and collaboration.
courses.description2: Personal Leadership provides a comprehensive introduction to leadership theory and practice, designed to help students discover their unique leadership style through self-awareness and practical skill-building. Through interactive workshops, reflective exercises, and real-world applications, students engage deeply with core leadership principles and develop the tools needed to lead confidently in any setting.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Genuine business/leadership/finance/legal/economics content; withdrawn from the former business-heavy alternative to restore defining biomedical substance.

courses.profile: Leadership & Diversity Management explores how diverse perspectives and experiences shape effective leadership in dynamic, varied environments. Blending cutting-edge theories with hands-on practice, students develop the skills to lead with empathy, inclusivity, and adaptability. Through engaging case studies, interactive workshops, and reflective assessments, participants build awareness of diversity and learn to inspire ethical, collaborative teams.
courses.description2: Leadership & Diversity Management explores how diverse perspectives and experiences shape effective leadership in dynamic, varied environments. Blending cutting-edge theories with hands-on practice, students develop the skills to lead with empathy, inclusivity, and adaptability. Through engaging case studies, interactive workshops, and reflective assessments, participants build awareness of diversity and learn to inspire ethical, collaborative teams.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Genuine business/leadership/finance/legal/economics content; withdrawn from the former business-heavy alternative to restore defining biomedical substance.

courses.profile: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.
courses.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Data handling, cleaning, visualisation and own research project; no full machine-learning syllabus established.

courses.profile: Image Processing and Computer Vision deals with extracting high-level structural understanding from digital image and video data. As such, it aims to automate the task of the human visual system. In the broadest sense, Image Processing and Computer Vision studies methods for acquiring, processing, analysis, and understanding of image data. The course starts with a concise introduction into cameras, color models, and various image models and representations, but focuses on the processing, analysis, and understanding of image data. Image processing and analysis have many applications, inside as well as outside of robotics. An important application domain is medical imaging, where the goal is to reveal internal structures to diagnose and treat disease. Another application is remote sensing which aims to detect objects on earth. Image processing and analysis study methods that turn images into better images and aim to identify simple features in images. The course considers histograms, point operators, and local, edge, and morphological filters. It covers the Hough transform for detection of lines and curves, detection of corners, shapes and regions, and segmentation. Image understanding concerns the recognition of objects in images. The course introduces feature detection and tracking and object localization, classification, and evaluation. The Image Processing and Computer Vision course offers ample time to practice with the image processing, image analysis, and image understanding methods that are presented.
courses.description2: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Digital-image processing, features and segmentation with explicit medical imaging application; does not supply complete non-invasive acquisition/instrumentation training.

courses.profile: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation.
courses.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Moral theories, practical ethical argument, essays/presentations; not the complete Philosophy in Action trajectory.

courses.profile: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.
courses.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Qualitative social research design, data collection/interpretation and positionality; companion methodology, not biochemical experimentation.

courses.profile: Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_ But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?
courses.description2:
Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_
But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?
courses.contributionAndLimit: Epidemiology, risks, disease trends and evaluation of public-health evidence.

courses.profile: Functional Anatomy examines the structure of the human body in direct relation to function. In this course, anatomical structures and their functions are systematically studied together, at the level of body systems as well as individual anatomical components. The course is organised in thematic blocks, each addressing a specific anatomical region or system (the Skeletal System & Vertebral Column; Bony Thorax & Pelvis; Respiratory & Cardiovascular Systems; Abdomen; Reproductive & Lower Urinary Systems) and each emphasising specific anatomical and functional reasoning (rather than exhaustive memorisation). Within these blocks, learning activities are purposefully selected to support the intended learning outcomes, combining visual, spatial and experiential approaches. Anatomical understanding is developed through surface anatomy, medical imaging, scientific anatomical drawing and video-based human remain based material, complemented by carefully framed encounters with human skeletal remains, a dissection facility and in class clinical demonstrations. Together, these activities foster three-dimensional anatomical insight, spatial reasoning and awareness of anatomical variation. Please note that these are explicitly framed as academic learning experiences rather than clinical skills training. Studying human anatomy inevitably confronts students with an ethical paradox: respect for the human body is taught through its objectification for scientific study.
courses.description2: Introduces human body functioning using imaging, surface anatomy and dissection materials. Shows how anatomy serves function and discusses ethical considerations of learning from the dead.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Functional anatomical systems, imaging/drawing/spatial reasoning and framed encounters with remains; academic, not clinical skills training.

courses.profile: Pharmacology is the science of drugs including their origin, composition, pharmacokinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity (Merriam-Webster Learner’s Dictionary). The functioning of the (diseased) human body can be affected by (medicinal) drugs, which act through a variety of molecular mechanisms. In this course, the basic principles of pharmacology will be discussed, followed by studies of different aspects of drugs and the human body to illustrate the se pharmacological principles which are used for rational drug develo pment and physiological use. The importance of neuronal, hormonal, immunological (whole body) and biochemical (whole cell) regulation for proper physiological and cellular function, and dysregulation during pathological processes are emphasized. Identification of potential drug t argets and the interaction of drugs with macromolecules (enzymes, cell surface receptors, and signaling molecules) as the main pharmacological principles are central in this course. Quantitative pharmacological, pharmacokinetic and statistical methods are used. At the end of the course you will be able to explain effectiv ely existing drug therapies in a rational way in terms of molecular targets, cellular actions and physiological consequences of pharmacological treatment. They will be able to suggest targets for drug development on the basis of pathophysiological insights a nd to apply pharmacological models when describing concentration-response, time-concentration, and time-response relationships of drugs.
courses.description2: Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Drug mechanisms, targets, pharmacokinetics, concentration/time responses and rational therapy.

courses.profile: Infectious diseases and disorders of the immune system are a continuous threat to the life and well-being of humans, animals and plants. Studying the fundamental processes in immunology, such as the recognition of self and non-self (e.g. microbes), development of mature lymphocyte receptor repertoires, and the innate and adaptive immune response is crucial for the understanding how the immune system deals with the daily threat of microorganisms. On the other hand, general knowledge of the highly diverse mic robial world is needed. From this knowledge, detailed specific understanding of microbial strategies to circumvent host resistance can be acquired. As a principle, the course will focus on interactions between host and infectious agents. Basic principles a s microbial virulence, inflammatory responses, tissue damage and apoptosis are discussed. In addition to normal immune responses to infectious agents, the course will also deal with immunopathological processes and diseases.
courses.description2: Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Host-pathogen interaction, innate/adaptive immunity, inflammation and immunopathology.

courses.profile: In this course the relation between the normal function (physiology) and disease (pathophysiology) is illustrated for six basal organ systems: 1. cardiovascular, 2. lung (pulmonology), 3. kidney (nephrology), 4. digestive tract, 5. endocrine glands (endocrinology) and 6. central nervous system. The aim of this course is to provide insight in the principles of the mechanisms of diseases. For the organ systems mentioned the student first has to study the embryology and anatomy, Using this information as starting point, the basic physiology is studied and using the combined knowledge the student must be able to derive the symptoms and failures in the system or the pathophysiology.
courses.description2: Examines molecular and cellular defects triggering pathologies. Presents clinical cases, discusses disease mechanisms and treatments across systems and includes an assignment to invent an imaginary disease.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Organ-system physiology/pathophysiology from embryology/anatomy to symptoms; not a standalone reproductive-development sequence.

courses.profile: Cognitive neuroscience uses inputs and perspectives from many disciplines, such as psychology, biology, medicine, computer science, and philosophy. In this course, the focus will be on the biology side of neuroscience. As a result, we will focus on evoluti onary pressures on animals in general, resulting in specific behaviors and physiological processes in these animals and ourselves. In this light, you will gain a greater understanding of biorhythms and natural behaviors, and eventually of specific disorders and diseases. Additionally, we will take a look at the use of animals in neuroscientific research, such as rodents, and discuss ethical and welfare implications. We will also familiarize you with experimental techniques in the laboratory, such as cell st aining and using a microscope, and compare the (brain) anatomy of different animal species. This course will familiarize you with concepts and skills required within the discipline of Neurobiology. A selected number of key topics within the field will be discussed, including comparative anatomy, biorhythms, animal models and ethics, and disorders . The course also includes guest lectures and practical work such as labwork, group assignments and student presentations.
courses.description2: Examines evolution and complexity of brains. Explores animal cognition, welfare and research ethics and studies how brain regions and rhythms regulate behaviour through interactive assignments.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Comparative/evolutionary neurobiology, biorhythms, animal models, anatomy, ethics and practical work.

courses.profile: Have you ever wondered what makes life on earth possible? The foundation of life, health & biomedical science course takes you on a journey into the building blocks of life, exploring how cells, molecules, and systems interact to create and sustain living organisms. Cells are at the heart of this story: they are the basic units of life, taking in energy and nutrients from their environment and converting them into biologically useful forms. Inside every cell lies genetic information, dna, that not only directs all cellular activities but also passes traits from one generation to the next. Mutations, recombination and epigenetics create variation, and this diversity fuels the evolutionary process through natural selection. The course is structured in four interconnected units: The cell as a unit of life Basic molecular biology Cellular physiology and communication Capita selecta (a series of explorations that give you a first taste of the diverse academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.) You will also work on a special research presentation assignment, which allows you to engage with scientific literature, reflect on how we know what we know, and experience how new knowledge can be generated. But this course is more than just an introduction. As a gateway course, foundation of life, health & biomedical science opens the door to exciting academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.
courses.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Biological cells, molecules, gene variation, cellular physiology and research literature; genuine biomedical foundation.

courses.profile: This 100-level course ‘Introduction to Brain & Behavior’ constitutes the Gateway Course for the Cluster Health, Cognition and Behavior: Units ‘Cognitive Science’ and ‘Clinical Psychology’. In this course you will gain foundational knowledge and essential skills that you will need in intermediate and advanced courses of these units. We will look at the various ways in which psychologists and neuroscientists have approached questions such as: Why do people behave the way they do? Can we predict behavior and mental processes in a particular situation, for example after brain damage? Is it possible to change these behaviors and mental processes? How do nature and nurture interact in the development of how we think, feel and behave? Which areas of the brain serve which function, and how do neurons communicate with each other and with the body? We will explore these complex and fascinating topics together from a neuroscientific and psychological perspective, learning about functional brain anatomy on a micro and macro scale, research methodologies and tools in the fields of Cognitive Science and Clinical Psychology, as well as main psychological theories and the relevance of main clinical skills in Psychology. The course will be organized including a combination of different methods of teaching and learning; e.g. interactive lectures, individual and team activities with a collaborative learning methodology, guest lectures, reflective activities, among others. Course outline HCBGATE102 Introduction to Brain & Behavior Page 2 of 16
courses.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Brain/neuron function, psychology and neuroscientific research methods; not full movement physiology.

courses.profile: New discoveries and advancements in scientific research are proposed every day, all around us. It can be overwhelming to keep up. This course provides the foundation for students to understand a vast array of practical applications in a multitude of life science topics (e.g. industry, medicine, agriculture, ecology, etc.). Students w ill take a closer look at the cellular biology of mostly eukaryotes, but also prokaryotes, gaining a comprehensive understanding of cell structure and physio logy. Concepts from the LIFE101 course, Introduction to Life Sciences, will be revisited and students will dive deeper into the details of life processes to understand the underlying molecular mechanisms. Students will also learn to examine current research topics and methods used to study the invisible world of molecular biology. Students will be encouraged to question the reproducibility of results and to propose how modernization of existing methods (and/or theoretical) technologies would improve the limitations of research and the validity of results. The course consists of five themes: 1 – The fundamental units of life: Cellular components, chemistry and energetics 2 – Genomes: DNA to Proteins, replication, repair and regulation of gene expression 3 – Cellular dynamics: Membrane trafficking, transport and signaling pathways 4 – Cell fate: Cell division, tissues, stem cells and cancer 5 – Drug Mechanisms (Paper and Poster Project)
courses.description2: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Substantive cell structure, gene regulation, signalling, cell fate and drug-mechanism analysis.

courses.profile: Physiology is the study of the normal functioning of a living organism and its component parts, including all its chemical and physical processes. In this course, the focus is on the function of the adult human body and of different organ systems. Knowledge of the subject is essential for students with a medical interest and recommended for every student interested in the function (s) of the (own) human body. The course includes fundamental concepts of molecules, cellular and systems physiology to understand how the human body functions and maintains a steady state. Although some medical examples are used to illustrate general physiological principles, this is not a course in medical physiology. Still, the core of physiological knowledge you will learn by ta king Human Physiology will help you better understand human health and disease. The course will be divided in 4 units: (1) Basic cell processes , (2) Homeostasis and control, (3) Integration of function , and (4) Metabolism, growth, and aging . In addition there will be one individual assignment. Contents of the 4 course units are structure-function relationships (organelles, cells, tissues, organs), energy handling, homeostasis and control systems, signaling and communication, study of individual organ systems (cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine, muscles, nervous, digestive, reproduction), and integration of functions.
courses.description2: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Normal adult systemic physiology, homeostasis, metabolism, growth and ageing; explicitly not medical physiology.

courses.profile: Living organisms evolved from the prebiotic world through chemical reactions. Laws governing those early reactions are the same t oday. C hemistry is the underlying science behind biology. Biochemistry, the chemistry of life, deals with the reactions that produce the molecules of life: proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids that enable the self -assembly and reproduction of simple and complex organisms. Although organisms vary en ormously in complexity and biological properties, all domains of life use similar biomolecules for encoding and transmitting information, intra - and intercellular signaling, formation of membranes, building and degrading macromolecules, energy metabolism, and many more features. Errors in the production, proper localization or degradation of these molecules can often lead to disease. Biochemical knowledge is not only essential for understanding and treating these diseases, but also necessary for advancing many applications in biotechnology.
courses.description2: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Biomolecules, biochemical mechanisms and biotechnology foundations.

courses.profile: This course is designed for a broad group of UCR students interested in life sciences. This course provides an introduction to the biochemical and molecular laboratory work performed in most labs today, and hence is a highly recommended course for all life science and medical track students. The students will be introduced to the following themes: • Blood • Bacteria, handling hygiene and genetically modified organisms (GMOs) • Protein production, isolation and analysis • DNA isolation and analysis (digestion, PCR and gel electrophoresis) • Bioinformatics These themes are characteristic or representative of basic biological and clinical research. Additional clinical diagnostic themes are added whenever there is an opportunity. The concepts, principles and techniques used in this course regarding blood and blood proteins include a basic blood cell analysis (hemogram), protein electrophoresis, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and a patient case. Course outline HCBLIFE214; Life Science Laboratory Page 2 of 8 With respect to bacteria, students will first learn the skills for properly handling pure cultures. A series of tests will also be carried out to check hygiene and sterilization procedures, bacterial species determination and the effect of antibiotics on bacterial growth. It also includes genetic modification of bacteria using safe microbiological techniques. After students have become acquainted with the safe handling of bacteria, they will generate a genetically modified organism (GMO).
courses.description2: Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Introductory molecular/biochemical laboratory work, blood/ELISA, bacterial hygiene and GMO techniques; not the complete integrated placement or competence assessment.

courses.profile: This course covers a vast number of topics from general and molecular pathology and genetics of humans. The pathology portion includes the bases of pathology which is cell injury and cell death. The pathology also covers how acute and chronic inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration and fibrosis, and neoplasia contribute to pathologies. The course then shifts to understanding the molecular genetics underlying disease. The significance of chromosome structure and organization of genes will be covered along with gene mutations (and their inheritance) through several examples of genetic diseases. The course also focuses on the status of genetic testing and genetic treatments. Ethical and legal considerations for now and in the future will also be examined.
courses.description2: Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Human pathology, cell injury, inflammation, genetics, testing/treatment and ethical context; not full reproduction/embryology training.

courses.profile: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in in medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers whether in data science, business analytics, market research, political science or sociology. The phenomena investigated by scientists studying humans are usually complex, thus multiple variables must be used to explain them. The theory and application of multivariate statistical models will be discussed. These models can be used to investigate the relations among many variables simultaneously, thus providing an accurate explanation of the subject of interest. The course introduces most used multivariate statistical models such as linear regression, factor analysis, analysis of (co)variance, and logistic regression. Furthermore, attention is paid to non-parametric tests. Practical application: you will learn to apply these models to data. In addition, learn how to deal with problems that occur when statistical models are used. At the end of the course, you will be able to determine which statistical model should be used to investigate different types of research questions. Furthermore, you will be able to execute the corresponding analyses and report results, conforming to APA guidelines.
courses.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Multivariate/regression/ANOVA/logistic and nonparametric models and reporting; stronger specific advanced-statistics relationship than general introductory methods.

courses.profile: The definition of what is a mental disorder is very complex, and there is no universal agreement about it. This course explores mental health and mental disorders across the lifespan, emphasizing a bio-psycho-social perspective that considers how biological, psychological, and social factors interact to promote mental health or contribute to the development of disorders. Students are introduced to historical and contemporary views of psychopathology, the prevalence and development of mental disorders, and the role of culture, gender, and environmental factors in shaping mental health and illness. The course familiarizes students with key concepts, terminology, theories, and research methods in psychopathology, while fostering critical thinking and analytical skills for evaluating mental health information. It addresses the assessment, diagnosis, classification, and treatment of mental disorders, including the most prevalent disorders from infancy through adulthood. Through interactive lectures, audiovisual materials, discussions, exercises, and written assignments, students gain a research-oriented understanding of maladaptive behavior and develop greater awareness of both their own mental health and the mental health of others within a comprehensive bio-psycho-social framework.
courses.description2: Provides a deep dive into factors shaping mental health. Teaches critical thinking, explores the bio‑psycho‑social approach and covers mental disorders, research findings and assessment techniques.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Biopsychosocial psychopathology across lifespan; companion mental-health perspective.

courses.profile: This course will introduce you to methods to perform systematic reviews and meta-analysis: the statistical analyses that are used to synthesize summary data from multiple of studies. Meta-analysis and systematic reviews are being used in many disciplines, including psychology, medicine, education, and others. Meta-Analysis and systematic reviews are very important tools in evidence based policy making as they allow to combine results of existing studies fairly objectively, to establish general treatment effect (effect size) and degree to which effect size is robust and consistent across the kinds of studies sampled. Participants will get hands-on experience in performing analyses using R. R is leading language in statistical computing. R is an open source language with huge number of individual and institutional users. The introduction to will help you the understand basics of R: program interface, syntax, variables and operations, reading data into R, accessing R packages, how to handle data structures, and create own functions. You will get acquainted with community developed packages providing common statistical analyses and practice conducting meta-analysis using R. The course is active learning oriented, with you presenting and performing preforming tasks in the class. As it is a 300 level course you are expected to take the responsibility for your learning and proactive attitude: come prepared to the class, complete homework/practice exercise and actively search answers to your questions and unclarified issues.
courses.description2: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Systematic reviews and meta-analysis using R across medicine and other fields; not an individual original biomedical placement/thesis.

courses.profile: How do we become unique individuals? Which factors influence this process and how do they interplay in each stage of our development during our lives? In this course we will explore these and many other questions about human development, where students will acquire knowledge and develop critical thinking and understanding of the main aspects related to human development throughout the lifespan. The main goal of the course Developmental Psychology is to introduce the student to the basic concepts, issues and me thods in the field, which is concerned with human physical, cognitive, social and emotional development throughout the lifespan: from pregnancy to infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and older age; their descriptions and understandings, as well as t he most relevant theoretical approaches and some psychological assessment and interventions in the different phases of life. Therefore, this course will address the following subject areas: 1. Historical and contemporary views, and main theories in Developmental Psychology; 2. Biological and environmental foundations of human development; 3. Pre-natal development and birth; 4. Attachment and physical, cognitive, emotional and social development in infancy. 5. Physical, cognitive, social, emotional and personality development in early and middle childhood, adolescence and early, middle and late adulthood; 6. End of life: death, dying, and bereavement.
courses.description2: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Physical, cognitive, social and emotional development across lifespan, including prenatal/ageing; psychological perspective, not complete biological developmental disease curriculum.

courses.profile: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. The course starts by considering the Greek and Roman Western roots of rhetoric. It focuses on the canons of rhetoric applied to the three main types of argumentation, i.e.
courses.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
courses.contributionAndLimit: Rhetorical analysis and academic written/oral argument; not full scientific communication/Endnote/MSF trajectory.

comparability: Two qualified programmes retain the same11-course biomedical core82.5EC: foundations, cells, physiology, biochemistry, laboratory work, pathology/genetics, epidemiology, anatomy, infection/immunity, pharmacology and disease mechanisms. The primary adds neurobiology, developmental/abnormal psychology, systematic review/meta-analysis, quantitative/image/data and qualitative enquiry. These are genuine related contributions, not a reproduction of the Maastricht competency assessments or internship. The reconstructed enterprise direction replaces the former business-dominant proposal: it retains all11 biomedical courses including laboratory, anatomy, publichealth and disease mechanisms, plus22.5EC research/statistics/data and52.5EC enterprise/design/marketing/accounting/governance. Seven exclusivecourses52.5EC each way establish a real change in organising question, with sixadvanced courses in each. Business courses are taught as general business/design, not verified medical-device development, clinical translation, regulatory approval or drug-commercialisation projects. Source5585 supports an entrepreneurship profiling direction, not replacement of the defining biomedical core. Current22EC integrated internship/thesis/defence, scaffolded professional/communication assessments, advanced specialist depth and complete biomedical imaging/acquisition and machine-learning content remain gaps. Elective30EC is open subject to approval, not an assumed compulsory immunology package. A third biomedical-education candidate was genuinely reconsidered: UCR Rhetoric in Action includes didactic training and teaching children public speaking; other communication courses include literary stylistics, climate communication, creative poetry/performance and general persuasion. This does not establish a distinct sustained biomedical teaching/pedagogy curriculum. The official stable minor direction is education; general communication is a core competence, not by itself a separately established science-communication minor. Rejection is substantive, not merely absence of a teaching credential. No degree, professional qualification, master admission or career equivalence claimed.
